speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: It was April 25, and at the present, he is the Culligan manager in Moscow; so, if you have soft water, John is who you call your troubles into.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: All right, now let's get back to you. How much schooling did you have?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Two years of high school.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And what are the special skills that you have? The things you've done at home and on the farm.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, just a wife and mother. I think I have always had a good relationship with my children. If I had any talent, it was keeping close to them. We were good friends as well as mother.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you do canning, preserving of foods?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, but I didn't like to.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: But you did it?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I had to, everything from meats, vegetables, fruits, and it wasn't a dozen pints or anything like that -- it was 50-60 quarts of peas! Go out in the field, my family helped me, they were the ones that went and picked, but I would shell. I say this wasn't just a few dozen pints, it was dozens of quarts; you put everything up into quarts and half gallons.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you had six children to feed through the winter?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, you see, our children were so strung out that they weren't, except to come home when they went to school and like that. I went to my 25th anniversary party pregnant. That didn't help any either, believe me .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That is a unique experience, I'm sure.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, I don't think there's too many that does that . But, I cooked and I baked and I canned, and I remember canning meat and we butchered hogs and canned sausage. We had everything that went on a farm. We made butter. We were always making butter; seems to me like I always had butter churning.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, now, when you butchered did you get right out there and help?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You took care of it after it came in the house?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I had wonderful help then. Our neighbors out there were bachelors, right next door, and they came in and helped me in the house until the last floor was scrubbed, the last pan.They helped me can, they helped me with everything. Dad worked good too and they were the Christensen brothers. They just went from one family to another helping them butcher.

speaker: Harry Egland
words: He would bring cigars.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: He didn't take the meat?

speaker: Harry Egland
words: No, he didn't take the meat or a thing -- he just bring me some cigars from town.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And when it was butchering time, they just came in and pitched in and helped you?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Of course, our neighbors came over for the day when we was butchering, but I never would forget all the help we would get . We had lots to do, wash boiler fulls of sausage alone and we'd stuff it, smoke it and then we'd can it . Make lard; we had a big kettle out in the back yard.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you make soap from that?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, but I didn't make all my soap but I did make quite a bit of it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You used lard for cooking and all, did you sell it?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No, we just used it for cooking. There wasn't any Crisco, we never bought that Crisco or shortening, we just used lard. We milked lots of cows and we had lots of cream handy. To this day, it's hard for me to cook without cream because I got so used to cooking with cream.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, then, you probably sewed, too, your children's clothing?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, I sewed, but the girls could sew better than I could. I never liked sewing. I wanted everything done; by the time I got everything done it was time to start something . See, we had three meals a day and two lunches. When the men would be in the fields, I had lunch out in the fields twice a day.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You took it out to them?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes . My sewing wasn't as much as cooking and canning and cleaning house and things like that .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Have you ever held a job or done anything like that?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Not to speak of. I went and worked in the peas just to see if I could. Dad said he lost money; he had to haul me in, bring me home and take me out for lunch every day. So it's hardly worth mentioning that I worked that for three or four months.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What was this now? [Two people, Irma Egland and Hollis Egland, enter the room. ]

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, hellow, Hollis! Come in, Irma! This is my grand daughter and this is my daughter .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: I heard that you were here, Hi! Hollis: We couldn't get in the back door.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: You should've just hollered. Irma, there ' s coffee out there in the pot. Irma: It's cold out there. I was tired of sitting at home . I figured it was worth it, anyway.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: I've just been having the best time asking her about her experiences and all kinds of things .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: She was just over sewing and working out. I said I couldn't say too much about either one of those, didn't do too much of it .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Now, I didn't get it quite straight exactly what you did in this job.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, years ago , they had ·a place where they packed green peas in Moscow and you did several jobs in there. You didn't sort them but you filled and you did everything to pack them in boxes using little bags of split peas . And it was the first year Harry came home from World War Two and he was at home, so he could cook supper for me and I got the children off ready to go. I worked maybe about four months .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How did you happen to get involved in this?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I just wanted to do something.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Just a change?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I just went into town one day. I never said a word. Dad and I called them up and asked them if they needed anyone in the packing room, I think they called it, and they said, "Yes, come down and fill in the forms." I went home and said, "I got a job." "What?" I said, "I got a job." He said, "How you going to get there?" I said, "You're going to take me ." So that's what I did one winter.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That's very interesting. But you only stayed with it for only four months?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I didn't make any money, but I did have the satisfaction of doing something. Don't you want any coffee, Irma?

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: We really got our schedules mixed up , I'll explain that. Did you have any hobbies through the years? Did you develop any hobbies? Did you have time for anything like that?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Since I've come into town I like to make things, Christmas balls, Easter eggs, various little things like that, nothing too useful but ordinary.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Have you been in any clubs?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, I am a member of the Historical Club in Moscow, the Happy Valley Club in Genesee and Grandmothers Club in Genesee. And I belong to the ALCW of the Valley Lutheran Church.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Have you done other things in the church that have been pretty important for you?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well , just being there and taking the children to Sunday School and taking offices in the ALCW.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you've had various offices in that?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Have you any [break in the recording here] . You were going to say something fascinating and as a matter of fact , it all is very interesting. So, just to make sure I don't miss anything, I just leave it on the whole time . Okay, you were talking about the ribbons and awards . You haven't really done that. Any other kinds of things that you can think of?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No. The youngsters got awards for this and that, basket ball, football, girl's state. My family was my thing. They were trying to get me to take bread up to the fair for years. Each year I'd tell them that I'd do it next year .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Okay. I'll get into some of the questions about your opinions and what you feel about things. What do you feel are some of the advantages or disadvantages of living in a rural area, in a farm or small town?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Oh yes, I think there's advantages. I think you keep closer to your children and I think you depend more upon your self for your amusements .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And you think that's better?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I think you have a closer relationship . Of course, I've never lived in town, this 12 years, 14 years , now this August that we've lived in Genesee. When John, our family was all grown up and gone, except John, who was ready for high school. I am satisfied that I raised them on the farm.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you know any women, have you observed anybody that lives in a big urban center?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No, I'm not qualified to judge.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: When your family grew up, how did your family life compare with what it'd been as you as a child?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, we had a most better friendlier relationship . As I say, I didn't grow up at home; I grew up all alone with my grand mother.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: It was a kind of special situation.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, it was different, and as I told you, we didn't even dare think, "I don't want to," with my grandmother, let alone say it. My children always felt they had a right to say their side of it. I always felt a little bit left out because I didn' t grow up being able to speak my side of it, of a question. So I wanted my youngsters to be able to, and I think they have .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What do you think about the differences between your children when they were growing up and now your grandchildren?

speaker: Harry Egland
words: It's dreadful now!

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, I think we've been very fortunate with our children and with our grandchildren, too . It isn' t always you'd like to have it be, but it's not me to say whether it's right or wrong.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Their world is kind of different .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, it is .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What do you think about the opportunities that were available to you, say when you were your granddaughter's age, compared to with your daughter had?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: They have much more opportunity now. We didn't know, we didn't expect because you just didn' t even think about it . And I think they have much more opportunities now, much more advan tages in school.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you ever consider not getting married, was that an option for you?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No, I don't believe it was an option to me.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You just decided you liked him so much that you were going to get married? Can you think of your reason?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No, I don't think I had a reason at my age . It was just something I wanted to do and it lasted for 53 years, so it must have been a good reason.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What did you expect out of marriage?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I didn't know what to expect. But I didn't think about it because I know I was awfully lonesome and I never thought I'd ever be lonesome out on the farm, but I was dreadfully lonesome.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: After you married?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Before your children came along?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, before and afterwards, too. Your children don't fill the entire thing that you need as an adult. At the time, we didn't go much, we didn't do too many things and the men worked out in the fields and came out feeling tired . So it was entirely different. If I had given it any thought , I didn't think of it like it was .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: When you first met your husband, where did you meet your husband?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: In Moscow.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What were the circumstances , do you remember? Irma: Some things, you don't really want to tell! [Laughter. ]

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That's okay, too, if you don't want to .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No, it isn't anything. I will never forget. It was a windy March day, I was walking home from the library. I went over to the library; I've always enjoyed reading, it was a hobby. My sister lived with, lived way down on East Sixth Street. I don't know if you know where the University of Idaho poultry farm is? Well , there was a house there then, and my husband was manager of that poultry farm, or foreman there. I lived with her and was going to high school in Moscow and just as I crossed the street, here this car stopped right in front of me! I had my arms full of books . He asked if I 'd like a ride and I said no, I wouldn't like a ride. But we started talking and we talked for a while and then he asked if he could come see me that night .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: [Talking to the photographer :] Should we stop now and take a picture? Is that what you'd like to do? [There is a lot of conversation between all people present about having this picture taken. The picture is taken and the conversation begins again between narrator and interviewer . ]

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Okay. We were talking about when you first got married. How long did you go together before you got married? EE : From March until October . But I went home, my folks lived up in Kamiah and I went home. Actually, after school was out in the last of May and Dad came up on the Fourth of July, I came up here again when school started again in September .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So you were a student when you first met him and you were still in high school and was he farming then?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, he was farming.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And then when you got married, you came directly to his farm?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, we was married in Asotin and we had Dad's car and we wanted my brother-in-law that went with us, that was my sister and her husband, to take the car and go because he had to be back at the poultry farm. We went up to visit my folks a few days before we married. He didn't feel like he could drive the car up the hill, the Lewiston Hill, so we had to come back. We were going to stay in Lewiston a day or two . So, that's kind of something, you know, then, people didn't feel safe driving a car because he wasn't used to it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Yes, that's pretty steep corning up that hill.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yeah, it was just about a little thing .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: The cars weren't as powerful.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No, they sure wasn't.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Didn't have as much horsepower .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No, that's true.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: I guess this would be a hard question to answer, but did marriage turn out pretty much like you'd expected?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I didn't expect, I was too young to expect; but, it turned out very well. I feel very at ease about it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You think you made a good decision?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I do .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And most of your children were born here at Gritman Hospital?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: All of them except my oldest one that was born up at my sister's .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You just didn't have a doctor available then?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, we went to Moscow all the time. You see our farm was six miles .. .

speaker: Harry Egland
words: Ten miles north . . .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Of Genesee, and Dad, Moscow was his town. Until the schools consolidated and we started to have more children and come to school activities here in Genesee and that was eight years after our oldest one. He was ready for high school when they consolidated. Dad was on the school board and, of cour se, some of them was against, thought we had a motive for wanting to consolidate. But we really felt because many times we didn ' t have school children enough to keep a school out in our district .

speaker: Harry Egland
words: I was working when our first child was born. I had a hard time putting her to sleep, I was out at the poultry plant.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Tell us about that ; I think that'd be interesting.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, we had a lady doctor that was a good friend that grew up right next door to us. She was my doctor, so she believed then, that was , Harry will be 53 years old this September. She believed Dad should be there . She said it'd be good for him to see what this is all about . I can remember her saying that . She says he was in the medical service all the time he was in World War One and she said, "You've had experience, so just go to work.11

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, she gave him the ether, he was the anesthetist .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: He gave me ether, and from then on we went to the hospital all the time.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What was the hospital's attitude then, towards you?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Oh, just fine.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Towards your husband? They kept him out of the way then?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No . I remember one time the doctor told him, because he had a tendency to black out, and they said to get out and get some fresh air . He couldn't come in the room at that time .

speaker: Harry Egland
words: That was a common thing . I spent all my time in France. I worked with a doctor, we cut off arms and legs. We had a pile outside the door, you know, a great big pile of arms and legs. It didn't bother me a bit . But, when the kids were born, the smell of that ether just knocked me out .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: But you were at hand when most of the children were born?

speaker: Harry Egland
words: Yes, I was right there . It ' s an experience some time . When the second son was born, I had a Model T truck and it stopped. I lost some part of it a couple miles from home .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: The doctor told me that Wally was gonna be born in August , and it was September 11, and I got tired of waiting. I'd stayed over with my folks a few days , but I wanted to be home . That had went on for over two weeks, so I went home and, sure enough, and it was pouring down rain, just pouring down rain, and I said L __ _  "Harry, things is gonna happen now!" We didn't have anything but an old Model T truck and there was some little thing, I don't know why it would stop in the first place, but you had to take it out and put it back in and then it would run and we got over on the highway and Dad stopped and he said, "I know exactly what to do." But he lost the little part.

speaker: Harry Egland
words: It was four o'clock in the morning .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: He lost the little part, so he walked down to the neighbor just a few yards and he towed us . He was the nicest, kindest man in the world, but also the slowest, and I sat there in the truck and I was really sick, and it took Charlie forever to get his clothes on, he was just so, he had to do it just so . And at last, he got there. It was his car and I got transferred to the back seat of that and we started to Moscow. He kept getting more nervous all the time and he was a very quiet man. But when we got to Moscow, he dashed out of that Ford and he opened the front door of Gritman's Hospital, and he started yelling, "Maternity case, maternity case!" You could hear him on the third floor .

speaker: Harry Egland
words: The lady that delivered us [unintelligible] , but the doctor charged for it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That ' s customary, I think.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: He's still alive, too, Mr . M in Moscow. He's still · --- there. He was our doctor, but poor Charlie, he was really excited. That was our Golden Wedding trip.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That was your present?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: That was when Mel was at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C. And Dad, he wanted to go on the train, he never wants to go anyplace by airplane, and the kids decided we should come . I get so tired that I wanted to go by plane, I didn't want to go by train. But, at last, Dad decided that we could and that was the route that we took. We was there for about five weeks in Washington.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Oh, that was a tremendous trip, wasn't it? You went through Valley Forge?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Oh, we did. There's a whole list of things . Melvin, he believes in seeing and doing everything that there is .

speaker: Harry Egland
words: We seen George Washington's bed and Martha's bed and the utensils they cooked with. Oh, they had fancy beds, you know, with the fringes around the top .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Oh, that was something! That really was a meaningful gift.

speaker: Harry Egland
words: New York City and Philadelphia ...

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: That was real strange when we was in New York City and the guy in the taxi asked Dad where he wanted to go . You see, Dad had been there the time he was in training. And he says, "Well, I'd like to go and see where the old hospital is that I worked in." We got in the taxi, Melvin had been stationed there, too, so he could do a lot of driving himself except that he took the car away. And Melvin told the taxi driver where we wanted to go. "Why," he says, "that's where the United Nations Building is." They'd torn down the hospital and they have the United Nations. So there was flags from all the countries and all kinds of, oh, policemen from all over.

speaker: Harry Egland
words: There were cops all around there.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: They really welcomed you, didn't they? Oh well, that is so interesting. Let me finish asking a few questions here . There never was a time, then, when you had to support the whole family, was there?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Oh goodness, no .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you ever worry about what might happen if your husband had died?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Never. He would, but I told him he was going to live t o be just the same age as his father, at least . Now, I've got three more years to go.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you never really lost any sleep worrying about how you'd manage? You felt pretty secure. You mentioned your community and church activities. What magazines or newspapers do you take now?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Oh, we take two daily papers, the Idahonian and the Lewiston Morning Tribune; we've always taken either the Spokesman Review or the Tribune and the Moscow paper . I get all kinds of magazines.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you remember some of the names of them?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Oh, McCalls and Good Housekeeping and regular family maga zines that we pick up at the store. House Beautiful, too. I love to read.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What suggestions would you give to a young woman who's going out on a farm, say, like you did? What do you think it takes to be successful?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: My suggestions wouldn't be any use to them because it's so different now.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What are the differences?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, electricity was the big difference. When I think of improvements, I think of electricity. To me it's still wonderful to press a button. Johnny was two years old when we got electricity, so we had been married, we must have been married 20 years, about.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Yes, we can figure that out.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I pumped the water, carried it in and carried it out .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You had kerosene lamps?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Kerosene, gas, whichever sprayed the light just up. We had gas, but I was scared to death of it so it was kerosene lamps. When I think of any one thing, I think of electricity. Then, we got water in the house, we got the pressure pump and it was just wonderful, electricity.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: I think you said your biggest problem was loneliness?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You didn't have any women that were close neighbors?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, all I did was go to school, you know.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Before you got married?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes , and I just wasn't prepared. Probably, I shouldn 't have been any more lonesome than any of the rest of them, but for some reason I think I was. But maybe I expected too much.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So that was kind of a surprise to you, how lonely it was out there and that's the thing you kind of remember, then.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: The worst part was lack of electricity and just kind of loneliness?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, I knew I wasn't going to have electricity, so I probably was used to electricity. I hadn't done too much work, my grandmother took care of that. Then this older sister of mine was kind of a mother to me too, that I lived with, she kind of thought for me and did for me. So, it was the loneliness that I remember having. I didn't know what the farm was, you see.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: It was a new experience for you?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, it was a new experience for me. It wasn't any worse for me than any of the rest, but I just wasn't ...

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Was it more work than you thought then?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I never minded the work. Oh, there were some parts that , yes, I minded it. I love to cook, I like to keep house; but I never did like canning -- it was messy and dirty and steamy. I never liked washing clothes ; I liked to iron. But the work was a minor thing.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How did you wash clothes before you got electricity?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: On the board. We had gas. The last few years before we got electricity, Dad had got me a Maytag that you could step on, but it was a gas motor. Before that, we had old washing machines, but mostly we used our hands .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: I remember the gas one was a little engine that went pop, pop, pop. Is that what it did?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Uh huh. Then we got electricity. They took the gas model in and put on an electric motor, so I still had the same washing machine. I had an automatic about the time we got John.

words: You've had a long stretch of experience. What TV programs do you like to watch now? What's your favorite?

words: Games . We like to watch games . We're really not TV people. We'll watch "Truth or Consequences."

words: You ever watch Groucho?

words: We do both enjoy the "Mike Douglas Show" because there's so many people on. We feel like we've met them, you know, after they've been on that show.

words: But you don't care much for the story type things?

words: Believe it or not, that would pacify the cows -- the radio .

words: No.

words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: As you look back now, was there anything particular that your husband would ask your advice about? Did he solve his own problems?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: He solved his own problems. I solved mine and he solved his .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So you kind of had separate areas where you made decisions?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes. He said the house was up to me and I'd run that , and he'd run the outside. I never bothered him.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you have separate money that you managed?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: We had a joint account .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And you just drew from it as you needed?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Uh huh.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you write checks as well as he did?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: There really was no decision about living on the farm, that was his business and you went there?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: That's right . And I still feel, with the girls , when they get married, the young men, maybe they don't look at it that way anymore, that they make the living, but I do. If they have a career, the woman accepts it and makes the best of that .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: She adjusts to that?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How did you decide to come into the town?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Well, that took a bit of doing . Well, I knew there was going to be, that there'd been problems all the time with John being a diabetic and I knew he'd be in high school and there'd be more sports and more things that he'd want to turn out for, and a lot of the times it was better for him to eat at home . Then, I was tired, it was six or seven miles of corning and going all day, all hours of the day and night, after school to pick up, you know, and to stay for , and different things. And I'd had it for five children. I said, I just want something. Be- cause that summer it happened that H_ _ _ and V_ __ lived here and they decided this house was too small for them and they had an opportunity to get a house out in the country for their family . So, they were going to move and I said to them (they didn't want to rent the house) , I said, "Would you rent it to us?" They said, "Oh, sure, we'd be glad to rent it to you!" So I said to Dad one day, when he was in a particularly good mood, "How would it be if we went into town for the winter? We could rent H --- and V_ __ 's house ." He didn't really listen to me too much. "Oh, sure," he says, "that's all right ." So, John and I had gone in, last of July, started coming into town, and we'd wash windows and we'd clean down the cupboards and everything. At last I said to Dad, "Now, I think we could do a load and you come in with the pickup." He says, "What for?" I said, "We're gonna live in town." And I said, "You said you would ." So , he came but his heart wasn't in it. The Washington Water Power man came as we was carrying a load down to the basement, and he says, "You know who's gonna live here, Harry?" "Yes," he says, "my wife and son." [Much laughter. J

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: He wasn't convinced yet that he was going to live in town.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: He still wasn't convinced. He did help me, though, and we got what moved we could, saying very little. Then, I asked the big boys , Harry and Wally (Harry had a truck) , to come home on Sunday and move all the big furniture, the washing machine and the dryer and those things, and they came. Even Harry, he was renting this house, his heart wasn't in it, they loved the ranch and didn't see why I wasn't perfectly satisfied then. Wally said, "I'll come and help you, but I don't know what you're moving for, but I'll help." And they moved us in. We had oil stoves back then and the radio and Dad's big chair . "Just leave those things here," he said, "I'll be out here and I'll be in town anyway." And we got in and got unpacked and got settled that night and he's never been sorry. He just didn't have the faith and he's found a corner where he ' s happy and I guess that took care of it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did he continue to go out there and farm?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, but you see he hadn't farmed the soil back, so there wasn't too much farming to do. If he'd been doing the work, I wouldn't of did it. But, with the farm all seeded down to grass and the soil low quality, there wasn't too much farming to do . It was quite a decision.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How did you determine how many children to have? Was that your decision?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No, you don't plan to have a child to go on your 25th wedding anniversary!

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: It just happened?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: It just happened for all six children, yes .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Is there anything, as you look back, that you would have done differently if you were to do it over again?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I don't know if I can say there is. Not that I think I was perfect or anything like that; but, I don't know what I could've done or either of us could've done. We had hard times as we've said, during the depression. But we didn't think too much about it, really, when you're eating well and living as you always have in this work and I always had one good dress and good shoes and the coat . Why, we didn't think too much about being so bad off. It's different in some cities I'm sure, and people actually going hungry; but we didn't . But what we could have done different, I don't know. I think we just did the best we could at the time.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You had your problems and you made best at the time .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Okay. That's all the questions I have to ask. Would you like to tell me anything else that we haven't covered?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I think we've covered everything.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: We've been pretty far, haven't we? Well, I've really enjoyed talking to you.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I have too, so much. It'll be 54 years in October now that we've been married.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That's really wonderful .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: We had the most beautiful 50th wedding anniversary out at our church, just lovely, we had the flowers. It was very hard, but we had to leave a little bit early because my son-in-law and daughter was going to Nepal and they could be here only in August, so we had it in August before our actual wedding anniver sary in October. And that was why our wedding trip was ahead of time because they wanted us to come while they was in Washing ton, D.C. I said, "Oh, it's harvest time, there won't be very many." We was talking to the lady that was going to cater and I said there won't be very many and she said, "Well, what do you think?" "I don't think there'll be a 100," I said. And there was over 200 people!

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you did have more friends than you thought . It must've been the whole community.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes. It was just a lovely party.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, I have a release form here and what it amounts to is that we've made this recording and you have an option of saying whether you want your name kept confidential, like, it will be put in the library and we might take out sections and put in our presentations. If you don't mind, we would use your name .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I don't mind at all . Photographer : And the photographs, too .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And the photographs, too .

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: They won't be good; I don't take good pictures .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You might be surprised. Okay, as the interviewer, I'll sign here.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: And I think that I would like it if in 100 years, some of my great grandchildren could go up there and listen to it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, they have the possibility.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: I'm so sorry that I don' t know more about my parents. Now, this is one thing, I think, anyway, it's different with my grand children. I don't know if I'm speaking for children as a whole, but maybe I was a little bit ashamed of it myself, the fact that I was born in a covered wagon and things like that . Maybe I had a little different feeling about it. But now, my children don't. They just think it's great, you know, and I think they know more, but I didn't know many things about my parents.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: They didn't share their experiences.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No!

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Like you were saying, you didn't ask your grandmother any thing.

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: No, I wouldn't think of asking! Well , when she told me that one time, my grandfather's sorrows , well, I just wouldn't of asked another question.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You always wondered about that?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes, and she had a book with his name in it from being in the service and I didn't ask her any questions about things that children now ask. I know our grandchildren really think it's great, a lot of the things their granddad can do . We talk about it and I think that's good.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So that's a big difference?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, I'll go ahead. You were saying that the material can be used at the discretion of the people in the project?

speaker: Etta Mae Egland
words: Yes.

words: Now, all of this is on the tape?
